You can't help but feel envious — why did your mother never do these things for you? You didn't take the coins, but accepted the candied fruits as a gesture of reconciliation. He, however, took it badly, snorted in scorn, and pocketed the coins for himself.

You can see through this man's false sincerity at a glance — he's no good sort. But you're no soft target either: when he offers you coins with false generosity, you accept them without hesitation, since he'd accuse you of taking them anyway, whether you did or not.

You can't help but feel envious‑how come your mother never did these things for you? You accepted the coins and fruits as a gesture of reconciliation. He snorted and sneered, confident and full of ambition, seeing you as his primary rival. Once he masters martial arts, you're doomed!

If it had been anyone else acting so outrageously, the sect leader would long since have driven them from the mountain gate. But this Martial Aunt was different — she had sat in the Scripture Hall for twenty years, laboring hard and contributing greatly to the Tang Clan, sacrificing her youth and missing her prime, until, nearing forty, a widower finally came to ask for her hand, giving her a place to belong at last. The sect leader had personally promised to grant her one wish, so long as it wasn't something that defied heaven's principles or betrayed their ancestors — the Tang Clan would move heaven and earth to grant it, and see her married off in style. Now that she'd returned, she poured that hard-won wish into this newly adopted son instead. Childless herself, she was utterly charmed by Chao He's endless flattering cries of 'Mother,' and lavished all her affection on him, hoping he would join the Tang Clan, master its martial arts, and never be bullied again. She ordered the sect's disciples to build up his standing, and hid her hard-saved silver beneath candied fruits for him to hand out and win over his fellow disciples — carrot and stick together, so that people would look at him with new respect.

At her command, the sect's disciples lined up in formation, splitting into two groups for a sparring session, exhausting themselves. The Martial Aunt showed her authority, content with the display, too lazy even to give a cursory lesson, and took her adopted son to the Zhengxin Hall to pay homage to the sect leader.

She assumed the man she'd handpicked was a master of her own training, and that disciplining you, an outside-surname disciple who'd never received the true teachings, would take no effort at all. Little did she expect your strange moves to come thick and fast — not that the senior brother had ever wanted to fight you in the first place, but even if he had truly meant to beat you, he might well have proven no match for you, and so he went down in defeat. The Martial Aunt was furious but had no way to deal with you. On second thought, she went straight to the sect leader to lodge a complaint, claiming you had secretly learned martial arts from another sect, and urged him to expel you from the clan.
Using someone else's hands to give you a proper beating, venting her spleen on her adopted son's behalf, only then did she feel satisfied enough to spare you, for now.

With reinforcements, the fellow disciples are now hesitant, yet you managed to overcome the odds with fewer resources. Since Second Senior Brother has taken action, he won't let them off easily. He announced that from now on, they must run around the mountain for morning exercises, double their daily lessons, cancel their lunch break, and meditate in Zhengxin Hall at night. The monthly exam has been changed to a biweekly one, and those who fail will be personally supervised by him. This life is surely worse than hell; even serving in the military seems more hopeful. Everyone is complaining loudly, and the Great Martial Aunt, seeing this disciple's harshness, fears provoking the crowd. After the show of force, she led her adopted son to Zhengxin Hall to pay respects to the sect leader.

Among the group of disciples, there are a few senior brothers who have been guided by the Martial Aunt, and they hold her in particular reverence. Though unwilling to fight you, they were compelled by the Martial Aunt's command to spar with you publicly.

With a single command, she intended to use the pretext of practice to order the fellow disciples to surround and attack you alone. Although the fellow disciples respected her, their respect ultimately outweighed their fear. They remembered her past hard work; it was one thing to occasionally show off on the mountain and make things difficult for everyone, but now she was absurdly trying to command her fellow disciples to beat up their own brother. This was unreasonable both emotionally and logically, and everyone wore expressions of anger, refusing to follow her orders. The Master Aunt had never been openly contradicted by her fellow disciples, and her face turned bright red with embarrassment. Unable to contain her anxiety, her arrogance diminished; she realized that if she continued to act tough, she would only ruin the matter at hand. Thus, she suppressed her anger and took her adopted son to the Zhengxin Hall to pay respects to the sect leader.

The Second Senior Brother has been disturbed for a long time. If the Great Martial Aunt only lightly scolds you a few times, he'd ignore it. But a married Senior Sister ordering disciples to surround and kill fellow disciples is something the Clan Rules cannot tolerate. He reluctantly intervenes, also using the opportunity to teach these unreasonable and foolish junior disciples.

Little Junior Sister saw you surrounded from afar and, without a second thought, took your side. Second Senior Brother had long since been driven to distraction by the commotion; seeing Little Junior Sister step in, he feared she'd come to harm over someone as worthless as you, and had no choice but to intervene himself, using the chance to teach these thick-headed junior disciples a lesson.

With a single command from her, all the brothers were compelled by her oppressive authority to attack you together, under the guise of sparring, while the Great Martial Aunt seemed intent on taking the opportunity to kill you.

Not long after the previous incident, Chao He once again came back to the mountain, this time with a powerful ally. He now walks with confidence, no longer the timid figure from before. The ally he has found is a senior master who was married into the Tang Clan, someone even the sect leader must address as his elder sister. Before the Third Senior Brother took over the management of the sect's accounts, this master was in charge, and every time she returned, she would display her authority, scold the younger generation, and satisfy her sense of seniority. This time, she is even more determined to assert her power, intending to give a severe warning to make her son's position clear.

You wanted to kill him so much that you honestly expressed your desire to kill him. Third Senior Brother was shocked, but the Sect Leader surprisingly showed a look of commendation and encouragement. Although they didn't allow you to kill him, beating him half to death was considered acceptable. Even the sect's senior masters supported you beating him. There was no hesitation. You grabbed his collar, took a big step out, threw him outside the courtyard, and then started beating him.

In the end you chose to let the matter rest, thinking that you were not so famous that people wouldn't talk if you pressed too hard, and so you let him off lightly. Third Senior Brother saw him down the mountain himself, and hearing him wail the whole way about his wretched luck, felt his pity stir; he gave the man the silver he'd saved through his own frugality, hoping he would find the will to better himself rather than bow to fate. Little did he know that the moment he was out of sight, Chao He sneered at him behind his back, thinking him an easy fool. Who was Chao He, really? Nothing but a con man, human trash, who never cheated the clever but preyed only on kind souls like Third Senior Brother. He cared nothing that his deeds spoiled the last of the world's goodness or made good people stop trusting others - he pleased only himself. He'd had schooling but never cared for it, and envied those who had, wishing every scholar in the world would die young and never be reborn.

This was the very line you had been waiting for. Seeing that even the Sect Leader wore a look of praise and encouragement, and that your own masters approved of you giving him a beating, you no longer hesitated. You grabbed him by the collar, strode out in big steps, flung him outside the courtyard, and only then set upon him.
Second Senior Brother then told you to go out with him and claim justice for yourself.

The Second Senior Brother heard this and immediately advised the sect leader to take the man as an inner disciple. You were startled and furious‑how could you, who had endured years of hardship without complaint, still be an outsider disciple? This man was using your reputation to act recklessly, yet the Second Senior Brother didn't even reprimand him, instead strongly recommending he be taken as a disciple. Chao He, with his thick skin, immediately wiped away his tears and laughed, showing no gratitude for such generous treatment, and even feigned reluctance, making you so angry you almost drew your small sword on the spot. Unbeknownst to you, the Second Senior Brother's tone shifted instantly, his face turning icy. He wanted this man to be accepted into the sect so he could punish him according to the Clan Rules. If he didn't torture this loathsome person to death, he would never change his surname from Zhao to Tang. Hearing this, Chao He immediately became humble again, making endless excuses, claiming his family had just passed away and he wasn't suitable for changing his surname, and began to play the victim. The Second Senior Brother was so eager to kill him that, in comparison, he found you, the real master, unexpectedly appealing.

This person used another's name to commit evil deeds. Although you didn't intend to retaliate harshly, letting him go would still leave you feeling resentful. You also dared not act improperly in front of the Sect Leader, so you consulted Second Senior Brother, the sect's chief executioner.

You listened to his confession and couldn't help but feel a deep resonance, seeing in him the humble version of yourself. You, too, had once suffered similar humiliations, been misunderstood, deceived, and fought desperately to defend yourself only to fail. Your wounds may have healed, but your heart was riddled with invisible scars. A flicker of compassion stirred within you, and you could no longer blame him. Even as a victim, you stepped forward to plead on his behalf, and the sect leader, seeing that he was not truly a Tang Clan disciple and could not be punished under the sect's rules, merely waved his sleeve and sent him away to rest in the inner chamber. You trusted him as you had once hoped to be a hero, extending kindness and compassion. Yet you had no idea that his gratitude was merely a mask, and his heart harbored a sneer, viewing you as an easy mark. Who was Chao He, after all? Known in Jianghu as Dirty Scum, he didn't deceive the clever, but only the kind‑hearted like you. He cared nothing for the purity of the world's remaining goodness, nor for the disillusionment of the virtuous. He reveled in his own wickedness, appearing humble and submissive on the surface, yet secretly wishing for your demise, hoping you would never be reborn.

The person was brought before Zhengxin Hall, where the Sect Leader was respectfully asked to preside over the hearing, with Second Senior Brother, the Chief Enforcer, assisting at his side. Even the ever-cold Second Senior Brother could not help but startle at the sight of him, and stepping forward to test him further left him even more shaken - for this was no disguise at all, but a face genuinely born this way. In truth, standing the two side by side, a close look showed they were not the same man at all; his features differed greatly from yours. He simply relied on others' reluctance to stare too closely, deliberately copying your dress and hairstyle, and out in public he was forever calling himself 'I, Zhao Huo' and 'I, Tang Clan Ugly Hero,' fooling those who had never met you or barely knew you. The moment he saw the Sect Leader, he dropped to his knees and wept aloud, claiming he too was a victim. The one he worshipped, he said, was some fake Tang Clan he never knew was false; selling the counterfeit medicine had been the senior brothers' doing; riding the horse that hurt people was not his choice either - he'd been forced onto its back and had been terrified himself; he called himself Tang Clan Ugly Hero only out of admiration for you; and as for calling himself Sect Leader, that too was others reading too much into his words. As for harassing virtuous women - he had merely stepped up to make conversation, and been mistaken for a lecher.

A large crowd gathered around the person on the training ground. You recognized their face, and it struck you like a bolt from the blue-this man's appearance bore a striking resemblance to yours. This was the infamous fake Zhao Huo, who had been impersonating you in Guangzhou, swindling people with counterfeit medicines. Now, he had gone so far as to steal coins from a blind beggar's bowl. Caught red-handed by the Beggar Sect, he attempted to frame you. However, Fan Xiaotian, with his sharp sense of smell, detected the pungent, mixed odor on the fake's body, realizing he hadn't bathed in days. This contrasted sharply with the subtle herbal fragrance that always lingered on you. Fan immediately declared him a fraud, sent the dogs on him, gathered the beggars to surround and beat him, then trussed him up and handed him over to the Tang Clan to claim a reward.

A crowd gathered around the person on the ground in the Training Ground. As you caught a glimpse of their face, it struck you like a bolt from the blue-this man, by appearance alone, bore a striking resemblance to you. This was the infamous fake Zhao Huo, the one who had been impersonating you in Guangzhou, swindling people with counterfeit medicine. Now, he had gone so far as to target a blind beggar, stealing coins from their bowl. Caught red-handed by the Beggar Sect, he was beaten and mocked, then trussed up and handed over to the Tang Clan for a reward.

On this day, as you were about to rest, Fan Xiaotian suddenly burst into the Disciples' Quarters, startling you. You thought that even if the relationship was close, there was no reason for him to suddenly enter another sect's territory, especially since you were about to remove your pants to change clothes and take a nap.

On this day, you were about to rest when suddenly a beggar rudely burst into the Disciples' Quarters. You were startled, thinking that even though the Tang Clan and the Beggar Sect have a close relationship, there's no reason for someone to suddenly burst into another sect's premises to look for someone. Especially since you were about to take off your pants to change and take a nap.

That day, as you were about to rest, someone came to announce that Song Bei, the Officer, was visiting. When you went out to see, it wasn't just Song Bei alone‑there were several official constables as well. You felt a sudden chill, thinking perhaps you had done something wrong. But Song Bei didn't accuse you; instead, he asked some strange and puzzling questions. One moment he inquired about your whereabouts, the next about whether you sold medicine, and then about whether you were married. Confused and bewildered, you couldn't make sense of it. It wasn't until Song Bei had the prisoner brought in and thrown to the ground that you recognized the face and finally understood why Song Bei had asked those questions. The man's name was Chao He, who had been selling counterfeit medicine under your name in Guangzhou, riding horses to injure people, harassing virtuous women in the streets, boasting about having a harem, and even claiming to be the Tang Clan Sect Leader. He had been reported to the authorities and arrested. Hearing of this, Song Bei, considering his friendship with you, had personally come to hand the prisoner over to the Tang Clan for your disposal.

On that day, just as you were about to rest, someone suddenly came to inform you that a disciple from the Cang Gang had arrived for a visit. You stepped outside to take a look, but did not see Shangguan Ying; instead, the Cang Gang disciples were escorting a person dressed in the Tang Clan's blue attire, tightly bound. They threw the person down, and upon seeing his face, you were struck with shock, instantly understanding the Cang Gang's intentions without needing further explanation. This person was none other than the impostor who had posed as Zhao Huo to swindle ten taels of silver from Shangguan Ying, and his real name was Chao He. Although Shangguan Ying did not come in person, she felt deeply apologetic towards you. She valued integrity greatly and, without you needing to ask, sent gifts worth hundreds of times the amount as compensation to the Tang Clan. Your fellow disciples were all grateful for the benefit you had brought them.

You ran into Shangguan Ying, who held out her hand and demanded money from you. You knew she was careful with her coin, but you never expected her to rob you outright. When you refused, she assumed you were trying to dodge a debt and produced a promissory note - written in black and white, plain as day: if this wasn't your signature for borrowing ten taels of silver, what was it? Full of indignation, you fetched an inkpad and brush, and Shangguan Ying realized at once that she had wronged you. The man who had borrowed from her looked just like you, and out of her regard for you she could not tell true from false; moved by old ties, she had lent him ten taels of silver without a second thought, never expecting to be swindled - she was furious to the core. The impostor, having pocketed the money, was surely quite pleased with himself, but he had not reckoned that Young Lady Shangguan was no one to trifle with. Devout in her Buddhist faith though she was, she lacked the grace to forgive a wrong three times over - anyone who dared cheat her out of money would be hunted down to his ancestors' graves.
I heard Ugly Hero Zhao Huo has turned up in Guangzhou too, hawking fake medicine under the Tang Clan's name, swindling people everywhere - and if they fall sick from it, he won't pay a cent.

After the incident, you and Tang Dajing were punished together by the Second Senior Brother with the Mournful Deaf Spider Punishment, your ears poisoned to the point of temporary deafness. Your wailing cries echoed through the Tang family courtyard, serving as a warning to fellow disciples and siblings.

The sect leader was accustomed to dealing with bullies and had dealt with quite a few. Regardless of their background, as long as they fell into their hands and their crimes were verified, the lightest punishment would be to chop off a finger as a warning, while the heaviest would be to execute them on the spot. When interrogating Tang Dajing, the leader had already entertained the thought of cleaning up the scum from the Shangguan family. As soon as Xu offered any evasive or perfunctory responses, he would be made to face the consequences of his actions.   Unexpectedly, Tang Dajing seemed to have no hidden agendas and recounted the whole story as if he were lamenting his misfortunes. He complained about everything from being expelled from the Cang Gang after his red rice was spilled, to being bullied by the locals for being an outsider. Despite being fresh fish and shrimp, they all refused to buy from him, calling him greedy. Xu Dajing had already suffered enough as a wanderer in a foreign land; there was no way he could maintain a friendly demeanor to make a living, which led to a violent confrontation and the subsequent troubles.  Upon hearing this, the sect leader understood the crux of the matter. It seemed that this person was too muddled to grasp the situation, still thinking this place was in Fujian, believing that without the protection of the Cang Gang, he could still haggle as an individual. Thus, the leader's intention to punish him softened. Xu could choose to turn himself in to the authorities or return to the Shangguan family to accept his punishment; if he refused both, he would face the penalties of the Tang Clan.   The implication was clear: they intended to take him in and regulate him according to the Tang Clan's rules. Tang Dajing was overjoyed, fearing that the leader might change their mind. Without further ado, he knelt down and knocked his head three times on the ground. He even took the liberty of changing his surname to Tang. The sect leader, seeing his straightforwardness, secretly smiled and did not correct him.
You brought him before Zhengxin Hall and explained what had happened. The Sect Leader stroked his beard and smiled faintly, quietly proud of you.

It's supposed to be two against one, but Fu Yun just chatters nonstop, offering no real help. Yet even without helping, his talk truly gets under people's skin—Xu Dajing's temper was volatile to begin with, so how could he not lose focus? You caught the opening it gave you and cut him down with your short sword.
It's supposed to be a two‑on‑one fight, but Fu Yun just chatters nonstop, completely not helping. Only after you lose does he suddenly strike and knock the opponent out.

You worked together to defeat Fu Yun, but were blocked by the local villagers, and someone even reported the incident to the authorities. Xu Dajing's claim of not fearing the authorities was just bluffing. Upon hearing that someone had reported the incident, he turned pale with fear and hastily pushed through the crowd to flee. But he had no coins, so he had no choice but to take out the secret manual from his body to sell to you in exchange for coins.

Pitiful isn't just your character, but also your skill—two against one, and you still lost, beaten black and blue and hauled back to Zhengxin Hall. The Sect Leader heard the whole account and was deeply disappointed in you.
To act bravely in the face of injustice is the very heart of chivalry—how could you stand idly by? You immediately stepped in, joining Fu Yun to fight that ruthless Cang Gang bully, Xu Dajing.
You bully the weak and fear the strong, yet you went to help that evil bully Xu Dajing, surrounding and attacking Fu Yun.

You went down the mountain and happened upon a crowd blocking the street outside a tavern, watching some commotion. Asking around, you learned that Master Fu Yun of Songshan was soliciting alms. Soliciting alms was nothing unusual, but what was odd was that he wouldn't pick on the weak—instead he went straight for the local tyrants who preyed on the villagers, provoking them with his sharp tongue until they were furious enough to raise their fists and strike.

You went down the mountain to move around and bumped into Li Fugui from the Beggar Sect. It was your first formal interaction with him. He was working hard to earn coins for the Outer Fort's renovation fund. You couldn't help but think, 'Can a beggar who earns his own coins through work still be called a beggar?' This thought you only dared to have in your mind and not utter out loud‑first, because you feared he might get angry and beat you up, and second, because you didn't want him to realize this and stop working hard.

Everyone knew you had been wronged, and that day they looked at you with a touch of sympathy. The Senior Sister ladling out the rice filled your bowl to the brim, drizzled it with pork lard, and hid a piece of fat pork at the bottom.

You were nearly wrongfully accused, and it's not that you weren't angry—you just knew he had someone shielding him, unlike you. There's no telling how he's so fortunate: when he errs, his godmother backs him, and when that's not enough, the sect leader takes the blame instead. You seemed to have reclaimed justice, but in the end your heart couldn't settle.

You were nearly wronged for nothing, and there's no telling how he's always so fortunate—when he errs, his godmother backs him, and when that's not enough, the sect leader takes the blame in his place. You got your justice in the end, but your heart couldn't settle. You ran off to the back mountain to roar and scream, not returning to the main courtyard until the sun was nearly down.

Since no one was injured, the incident could be considered minor or major, but the one being wrongfully accused is of little importance. Chao He figured no one would stand up for you, so he decided to hide for a few days to avoid attention, waiting until the incident faded and everyone's anger subsided before reappearing as if nothing had happened. Even if someone did pursue the matter, he could at worst cry, slap himself, and no one would dare take his life, would they? His calculations were largely accurate; everyone feared trouble, and as long as they denied it, the Tang Clan could not force a confession. By the sect's own rules, they truly could not torture a confession out of anyone, and without solid evidence, even the Chief Executioner had no leverage over him. Fortunately, he brought this upon himself by being arrogant and ignoring orders, failing to respond to three summonses without cause, which amounted to a grave insult to the sect leader, committing the crime of disrespect. It was only then that the Second Senior Brother had a legitimate reason to apprehend him and bring him back to the mountain. Chao He thought he could hide in plain sight, believing that if the Tang Clan wanted to force the issue, he would simply roll on the ground and wail until the whole neighborhood came to point fingers. But little did he know that the Ruthless Young Master earned his name for good reason—the trick did him no good at all against the Second Senior Brother, who broke both his limbs in the street with the Tendon-Severing, Bone-Dislocating Hand technique, then paid coins to have him bound and carried back up the mountain. Chao He's godmother, Tang Xiaolou, heard the news and left her business behind, rushing to intervene. However, no matter how she pleaded, the Second Senior Brother remained unmoved, allowing her to follow him all the way to the mountain and storm into the Zhengxin Hall, filing a complaint against you and the Second Senior Brother. She wept and pleaded, accusing you and the Second Senior Brother of cruelty and tyranny, defaming her godson, and begged the sect leader to take action, expelling you and the Second Senior Brother from the sect. But such lies would not fool the sect leader, who was no fool. Having already made an exception to admit Chao He into the sect out of consideration for a fellow disciple's bond, he could not let her recklessly twist right and wrong. Yet he was too sentimental, and recalling old times, he could not bring himself to be harsh. He could only take the blame in Chao He's place, and, sect leader though he was, ask the Chief Executioner for punishment. Tang Xiaolou had always judged by person rather than by matter, prone to favoritism; having no children of her own, she had taken in this sweet‑talking godson, hoping he would care for her in old age, which is why she doted on him so. But then, wasn't the sect leader also her kin, one who had studied and grown up alongside her in years past? Whatever reasonable advice others offered, she dismissed as nonsense, until the sect leader was hurt on account of her willfulness, and only then did she finally come to her senses a little. Leaving the Zhengxin Hall, she found Chao He still sniffling, his limbs only just reattached, asking her at once whether she had gotten you and the Second Senior Brother expelled from the Tang Clan. She flew into a rage and slapped him across the face. Yet she was always soft‑hearted toward her own, and seeing him cry again, she couldn't help but pity him, coaxing him gently and leading him down the mountain—though she silently resolved that this would be the last time. Chao He, the instigator of it all, came away unscathed in the end, while the Beggar Sect's Li Fugui and Songshan's Fu Yun, feeling guilty, stayed on at the Outer Fort to help repair everything that had been smashed and burned.

Fortunately, Third Senior Brother is a sensible man; the moment he thought it over, something felt off. Committing the crime yet deliberately leaving a signature—this trick sounded familiar. Could it be that the same habitual framer, forgetting you're on your own ground here in Shu, wanted to try his old trick again and pin it on you?
The blame is directed at you, you feel an unbearable sense of injustice, enduring all sorts of suffering, always trying to be a good person, yet this is the consequence?

The blame is directed at you, and you feel utterly wronged. If you had done something wrong, that would be one thing, but you haven't gained any benefit and are still being unjustly accused. How can this be acceptable?

Investigating the original perpetrators, both culprits showed a bitter expression, at a loss for where to begin. At that time, a monk and a beggar had indeed stolen a cake, but Fu Yun's act of taking Li Fugui's cake carried deeper meaning. It was not bullying, but rather an attempt to clear the Beggar Sect's reputation. He wanted the neighborhood to see: even if the sect's heroes were hungry, they would still strictly uphold chivalry, resolutely refusing to bully the people. Originally a noble tale, it was twisted by malicious individuals who seized the opportunity to spread rumors and incite conflict. Working behind the scenes, Chao He railed against the Beggar Sect's misdeeds before the Songshan monks, while slandering the Songshan disciples to the Beggar Sect's people. This eventually led to a major disaster. That man was timid by nature, becoming arrogant the moment he wasn't involved. In reality, he incited conflict between the two sides without considering the consequences. His motive was shallow, purely out of resentment, aiming to ruin your reputation. For that reason, he didn't care how many might die. In the end, the blame would fall on you, and even before the King of Hell's throne, he would deny any connection to those deaths, blaming you entirely.

You intervened without leave, and sure enough they set their old feud aside and turned as one, fighting your Tang Clan in shared fury. Third Senior Brother was fretting over how to end it when word came that someone had set a fire, and panic seized him all the more. Fortunately, all three parties were people of chivalry at heart—the instant they saw the commoners in danger, they turned swords into plowshares and fought the blaze together.
You died in the chaotic battle and became the sole casualty.

You intervened without leave, and sure enough they set their old feud aside and turned as one, fighting your Tang Clan in shared fury. Third Senior Brother was fretting over how to end it when word came that someone had set a fire, and panic seized him all the more. Fortunately, all three parties were people of chivalry at heart—the instant they saw the commoners in danger, they turned swords into plowshares and fought the blaze together.
You can only grit your teeth and risk being killed by your fellow disciples to stand on the opposing side.
But you let his words go in one ear and out the other, and turned right around to make common cause with your fellow disciples against the enemy.
He had no choice but to leave it to you to calm your own people, while he went to reason with whoever had started the trouble.
Third Senior Brother couldn't control the situation at all.

Your Tang Clan's method is to Fight their mother. When people are full and too idle, they will fight among themselves, but in the face of natural disasters, they tend to unite. The easiest way to reconcile the Beggar Sect disciples and the Songshan monks is to transfer the conflict, and thus it falls on the Tang Clan to personify the disaster without hesitation.
Mediating disputes is the Nangong Family's specialty, but Lu Weng approached the Tang Clan instead. That's great; the Tang Clan also has their own methods of mediating disputes.
Mediating disputes and being a peacemaker are the Nangong family's duty. Yet Lu Weng approached the Tang Clan, and no matter how you think about it, you feel uneasy.

Only when Third Senior Brother explained did you learn there had been trouble at the Outer Fort, and Lu Weng had come up the mountain for help. As with most Jianghu disputes, the cause was so trivial it was infuriating, yet Jianghu folk run hot-blooded — one wrong breath and an argument escalates, and once tempers flare, out comes a blade and someone dies. Even Daoist priests and monks are not above it. And this time it was monks and Beggar Sect disciples fighting over alms, contesting not just pride but their next meal.

Second Senior Brother is not like Third Senior Brother, who sticks to convention — he could easily guess where the trouble had started. He ordered you to take your bedding and move into the alchemy room to tend the fire in his stead, partly for the sake of the pills, and partly to keep you from further complications caused by the disciples' idle gossip. The moment he came down the mountain he had already tracked down Chao He's whereabouts, and stayed at an inn keeping watch for several days, only making his move once the sect leader had sent for him three times with no response.

Even though Second Senior Brother finds you displeasing, as Chief of Punishments he remains impartial and unyielding. Unlike Third Senior Brother, who clings to convention, he can easily guess where the trouble started, and has no energy to waste on someone as unimportant as you.

You never expected that even lying at home, trouble wouldn't leave you be. When your fellow disciples came back down the mountain, they all wore strange looks on their faces, and from Third Senior Brother you learned why: Songshan and the Beggar Sect had come to blows, and word was that you yourself had stirred it up. You were utterly baffled and full of grievance, and at once thought of the prime suspect — who else in the world would impersonate you but that repeat offender Chao He? Third Senior Brother didn't doubt you, but for fairness' sake he still had to take you to the alchemy room first to report to Second Senior Brother, while sending another disciple to summon Chao He up the mountain to confront you.

Senior Brother, tasked with rounding up men for corvee duty, came into the room and found you asleep. He was about to give you a scolding, but then thought of how you'd been busy from dawn to dusk lately with never a moment's rest, and felt a pang of pity. So he shut the door again and let you sleep. You slept clear through from noon until dusk, undisturbed by anyone, as soundly as you ever had. Well rested, you felt life brimming with hope once more.
You still wanted to pretend you hadn't heard, so Senior Brother charged into the room, gave you a beating, and dragged you out.
That day the weather was fair and mild, and just as you were about to nap, someone outside called out that corvee duty had been announced.
That day you were worn out in body and mind, and just as you were about to nap, someone outside called out that corvee duty had been announced.

That night, Ye Yunzhou sat in the forge, holding his sword and enduring till dawn without moving. You opened the window to see him seemingly deep in sleep, but in reality, he hadn't dared to truly close his eyes for even a moment. Just as you did not trust him, he did not trust you either. Early the next morning, he went into the mountains to split bamboo and build a simple thatched hut, then went to fetch his sister Yunshang to live with him. However, he was met with cold rejection; Ye Yunshang was now favored and living a life of luxury, enjoying fine food and drink, and had no desire to suffer alongside her brother in a grass hut.

After that, Ye Yunzhou sat in the forge holding his sword, enduring the night awake. You opened the window to watch him, motionless, seeming deeply asleep, yet in reality he hadn't slept at all. Just as you did not trust him, he did not trust you.

But seeing how well you got along with Ye Yunzhou, the disciples reconsidered — if even someone like you could be friends with him, maybe this Diancang swordsman wasn't so bad after all. Besides, since Diancang wanted him too, an enemy's enemy was a friend. Though their suspicions weren't entirely gone, they didn't turn him away outright, and let him spend the night in the disciples' quarters. Ye Yunzhou smiled faintly at the laughter and horseplay, for Diancang folk were usually so solemn, rarely so carefree. Yet he never guessed the Tang Clan's lively atmosphere owed largely to the Eldest Senior Brother's influence, with everyone picking up his cheeky, motor-mouthed ways.

Ye Yunzhou also knew this was a delicate matter, so he volunteered to stay overnight in the forge, waiting until he had finished building the thatched cottage before moving out of the main courtyard, to put everyone at ease.
Ye Yunzhou also realized the difficulty of this matter and volunteered to stay overnight in the forge. The next morning, he would move into the Outer Fort.

The sect leader dismissed the attendants and engaged in a deep conversation with the Ye siblings. Moved by their ancestor's loyalty, he disregarded the Second Senior Brother's advice and decided to keep the two siblings within the Tang Clan, offering them protection. He summoned the Junior Martial Sister as well, noticing her age was similar to Ye Yunshang's, intending to have them stay together. That night, Ye Yunshang slept with the Junior Martial Sister and the other female disciples. Since female disciples generally had fewer conflicts with Diancang, their preconceptions were shallow. Seeing Ye Yunshang's ethereal beauty and charming demeanor, they all found her likable. Ye Yunzhou, however, did not share this fortune. As his reputation grew, the Tang Clan's senior brothers and sisters grew increasingly anxious, fearing he might be stabbed to death by a single sword in the middle of the night.

The sect leader dismissed the attendants and had a deep conversation with the Ye siblings. Though he intended to retain them, he noticed from their words that Ye Yunzhou seemed inclined to leave, so he did not insist. Instead, he gave them several pills. After dinner, before it was completely dark, he ordered Third Senior Brother to escort them down the mountain.

The sect leader dismissed the attendants and had a deep conversation with the Ye siblings. Though he intended to retain them, he learned from their words that Ye Yunzhou seemed inclined to leave, so he did not insist. He only gave them a few pills, and after dinner, before it was completely dark, he ordered the Third Senior Brother to send them down the mountain.

Ye Yunzhou and Ye Yunshang had never encountered someone so decisive in their actions. When facing enemies, they were hateful and terrifying; when allies, they were respectable and awe‑inspiring. Though both situations evoked fear, the feelings were entirely different. After the matter was settled, the sect leader returned to the Zhengxin Hall and sent the Fourth Senior Brother to invite the Ye siblings to discuss things, including the Junior Martial Sister. As for you, you were instructed to clean up the mess and cook meals.

The Sect Leader immediately summoned Ye Yunzhou. Seeing him bow respectfully with hands clasped, the Sect Leader nodded and first asked about his background. Ye Yunzhou hid nothing and laid out his lineage: his great-grandfather had indeed served under Lord Yue Yun, military governor of Wukang, with the Listening Cloud Sword as proof.
Though the Sect Leader resented the corrupt court's oppression of the people, he held loyal ministers and filial sons in the highest regard. He reasoned that for the Ye family's ancestor to have followed Lord Yue Yun and won his trust, receiving the treasured Listening Cloud Sword, he must have served with great toil and unwavering loyalty.
He resolved in secret to protect the two siblings, making an exception to act as mediator and settle their dispute.
With the Sect Leader backing him, Ye Yunzhou dared to speak before the crowd. But after only a few words, doubting voices rose on every side. At the sight, the Sect Leader spoke one calm line: whoever dares interrupt again will have their mouth torn off.
Across the vast training ground, silence fell at once. Everyone thought the same thing: was there ever a mediator so fierce?
Ye Yunzhou's spirits lifted, and he gave voice to all his pent-up indignation. King Wumu had served the crown with utter loyalty and devotion — he would have spent every last coin on grain, armor, and horses. Where would he have found treasure to hoard?
Even if the people of Henan lined the roads bearing incense in his honor, how much wealth could those already plundered by the Jin still have left to give?
King Wumu had died eighty years past. Even if the legend were true and the treasure real, the Yue family had not died out — why would it still sit unclaimed to this day?
And consider the Red Peng King, Mr. Zeng Wen, Zhang Xian, and Xu Qing — which of them was not a commander fit for great responsibility? Lord Yue Yun, wise all his life, would never have entrusted something so important to a mere guard of the Ye family's grandfather's generation.
As for the talk of a tattoo, that was nonsense too — no one even knew where the rumor began.
Every word of this he spoke earnestly and in good faith.
But who among those present was willing to listen? Strangers doubting him out of greed was one thing, but even those who always called him brother pressed him just as hard — enough to chill the heart.
Ye Yunzhou's words rang out clear and reasoned, leaving the crowd exchanging uneasy glances.
Yet after a moment's silence, they still would not let it go, insisting in the name of the greater cause that even if there truly was no treasure, he should still prove his innocence. What they meant, in truth, was that Ye Yunshang should strip and be searched.
They reasoned that with righteousness on their side, sacrificing one woman cost them nothing — she was not their own sister, after all, and a ruined reputation was no great loss; at worst they would all apologize afterward and find someone to marry her off.
Ye Yunzhou was like a scholar facing soldiers, unable to make himself understood, furious and mortified. He longed to draw his sword and cut a path through the crowd to vent his fury, but among them were old friends of his — how could he bring himself to strike?
The Sect Leader only warned him to choose his friends more carefully from now on, then let him go.
As mediator, he was bound to preside fairly, judging the matter on its own merits, favoring neither side. Having heard the whole affair from the sidelines, the Sect Leader found not a single claim among them worth crediting.
Words were for those worth speaking to. For fools who could not tell right from wrong, and for shameless wretches hiding greed behind a righteous cause, only the blade would answer. Any who still wished to argue were welcome to come and stake their lives on it.
The crowd, cowed by his presence, quailed; those with any shame left cooled down and felt their faces burn, cupped their fists, and took their leave. Those who still refused to yield were hauled out by the old hands of the Jianghu loitering outside the courtyard gate — the Sect Leader had already ordered them gone, and to linger any longer meant only death.

Amid the clamor, the crowd elected a young monk of the Songshan Sect, hoping the sect's lofty reputation would temper the old devil of the Tang family's arrogance. The Songshan disciple stepped forward, raised a single palm in greeting, and introduced himself, but the Sect Leader asked first where his teachings came from — the Henan Songshan, or the Fujian Branch? At this the young monk's face clouded. He had taken his vows and been ordained in Qianzhou; his master hailed from the main branch in Henan, but since he himself had always lived in the Song state, he had never once set foot in the mother temple at Songshan — and he knew Henan lay under Jin occupation, its sacred hall in ruins, still raising funds to rebuild to this day. Among the heroes of the Central Plains this was much discussed: everyone knew Fujian Songshan was wealthy while Henan Songshan was poor. Some even argued that Fujian Songshan was the true Songshan Sect of the Song state, and that Henan Songshan no longer deserved to be counted among the Six Great Sects. Even so, a monk does not lie. Steadying himself, he still affirmed he was a disciple of Henan Songshan. Unexpectedly, the hostility on the Sect Leader's brow melted away, and upon hearing that his master was Chan Master Qinghai, his whole manner warmed, quite unlike before. Old and young then spoke together as equals, tracing the affair back to its roots — to how King Yue had been destroyed by treacherous ministers and a foolish emperor, and met his end at Fengbo Pavilion. Both sighed long and bitterly at heart, that so peerless a hero could not outlast men's scheming. The young monk, ordained under Henan Songshan, felt a deep debt of gratitude to Yue Fei and longed to do something for Henan's counties. He had come to urge the Ye siblings to bring out the treasure and fund the Imperial Court's war against the Jin, to reclaim Henan and bring Songshan back into the embrace of the Central Plains. The Sect Leader was unmoved by this: the Song state was already wealthy enough, while it was the Jin who were beset on every side and struggling to get by. That money would do nothing to break the Xiangyang front, and if the treasure really were handed to the Imperial Court, it would only buy the ministers and local officials a few more mansions, a few more fine horses, and a few more pretty wives and concubines. His questions done, he let the monk go, and the crowd, seeing the monk leave unharmed, quietly let out a breath they'd been holding.

Amid the clamor, no one could be agreed upon for a long while. Then a fierce constable, claiming the highest standing and the most rightful claim, shoved through the crowd. This one counted as half a Jianghu figure, and long used to bullying the common folk on the strength of a constable's badge — ordinary Jianghu folk dared not clash with the authorities outright and usually gave way — had grown all the more contemptuous of Jianghu people for it. They meant to strike first and cow the room, swinging their broadsword through the air a few times and bellowing, "You insolent rabble, what do you think you are? Looking to rebel?" — and were promptly sent to their next life. The officials who had come today were not this one alone. Anyone with any standing knew the Tang Clan was a thorn in the Imperial Court's side — not because of any grudge against the House of Song, but because the Tang Clan had been at odds with officialdom since its founding. This family surnamed Tang fit the charge of "using martial force to defy the law" better than any other in the realm; they had crossed swords with more than mere officials — even the Imperial House itself, back when Emperor Xuanzong of Tang tried to throw his weight around in Shu, only to have the Tang Clan, based in their Outer Fort, strip every last shred of his imperial authority. This constable had not only mouthed off but drawn a blade to threaten the Sect Leader — so he had asked for exactly what he got. When the crowd was told to put forward one more speaker, this time no one dared step up. Out of patience, the Sect Leader simply pointed at random and picked a thick-browed, big-eyed Beggar Sect lad. Li Fugui, of the Beggar Sect, wore an honest, simple face, and dropped to his knees the moment he stepped up — everyone assumed it was fear that drove him to such a deep bow. Then he blurted out the truth himself: fear it certainly was, but he hadn't knelt out of courtesy — his legs had simply given out. The Sect Leader had to hide his amusement, his temper cooling several degrees; he found he didn't dislike this blunt, unpolished young man at all, though he kept up a stern face and barked out his questions. Startled by the Sect Leader, Li Fugui spilled everything he knew and thought without holding anything back — from the treasure legend to the Beggar Sect's real purpose, even blurting out that the Gang Leader had specifically ordered them to be wary of the Tang Clan. Only half a beat too late did he realize what he'd said, and his face went ashen as he remembered the constable's grisly end; his eyes rolled back and he fainted dead away from fright. In truth, for all his ruthlessness, the Sect Leader was a reasonable man, and only ever killed those who truly deserved it; anyone who showed the least courtesy or sense would never be killed outright. He rather liked this Li Fugui, and besides, he'd heard the Beggar Sect had been sent by their own Gang Leader, who didn't believe in the treasure at all — they had only come to secretly protect the Ye siblings — so there was no reason to harm him. He called the Beggar Sect disciples over to carry Li Fugui off, and even gifted him a Dragon and Tiger Vigor Pill as a mark of favor. With the constable as a point of comparison, Li Fugui merely fainting was no disgrace at all — word soon spread instead that he had withstood Sect Leader Tang's invisible hidden weapon, and that fainting rather than being torn limb from limb only proved the depth of his skill, earning him no end of praise.

Feng Shi could have slapped himself for ever setting foot in that courtyard, but it was too late for regret now. The Sect Leader questioned him, and he dared not refuse to answer — he laid out everything he knew of the treasure rumor. He wasn't truly a bad man; most of what he did stayed within the bounds of chivalry, and he even tried to excuse the young men, noting that while some were greedy, plenty truly meant well, hoping to convince the Ye siblings to give up the treasure to help the crown fight the Jin. Knowing his life hung in the balance, he held nothing back, and did not even try to hide that he'd meant to play the peacemaker himself — mediating for a cut of both the money and the girl. Hearing him tear down his own reputation like that, the Sect Leader was finally satisfied, and let him go. Feng Shi thanked him over and over, fled the compound at once, and declared he would retire from the Jianghu — and he really did, settling far from the Tang Clan to live out his years in peace, never again breathing a word about the Tang Clan's fortunes, good or ill.

The crowd argued for a while and settled on the most renowned and skilled Great Hero present — Feng Shi, famed for his Cotton-Wrapped Embroidered Spring blade technique. His name still fell short of the Tang Clan Sect Leader's, but he was well known in his own right, often ran with the younger crowd, and was well liked. People called him 'Brother' this and 'Brother' that, and Feng Shi groaned inwardly, forced to grit his teeth and go along, hoping that after all these years the Old Demon of Tang had forgotten the past — otherwise, just for barging into the Tang Clan on impulse today, his life would be forfeit. Unfortunately, the Sect Leader had not forgotten. This man had once spoken ill of the Tang Clan, and the Sect Leader had hunted him a thousand miles for it; only the Nangong Family's intercession, and the fact that he had done nothing else truly wicked, had spared him death — he had been given a sound beating and a warning instead, that if their paths crossed again he would be torn limb from limb. In truth, had they simply crossed paths in the Jianghu, the Sect Leader would most likely have found him tiresome and pretended not to know him, letting him go his way.
